Society & Human Rights
• Hong Kong courts handed multi-year prison sentences to Tiananmen vigil organizers under the national security law, underscoring Beijing’s tougher stance on dissent.
• The UK will again debate an assisted-dying bill as campaigners simultaneously call for urgent improvements to palliative care.
• On the 25th anniversary of 9/11, memorials across the U.S. reflect on victims and the attacks’ complex social legacy; a study also finds June heatwaves forced UK school closures, costing 15m teaching hours.
• A tourist coach crash in the Swiss Alps killed five and injured dozens, and South Africa agreed to extradite six Nigerians to the U.S. over alleged romance scams.
Why it matters: A string of court decisions, policy debates, and crises highlight tensions between civil liberties, public safety, and the social impacts of climate and extremism.

Geopolitics & Diplomacy
• BRICS leaders meet in Delhi amid internal divisions and an outsized U.S. shadow, tempering hopes for a unified stance against Washington.
• Iran and Gulf states will convene to explore a temporary Hormuz shipping agreement, as regional actors seek to ease tensions and reopen a vital chokepoint.
• Djibouti will sign the Artemis Accords, becoming the 72nd country to endorse U.S.-led norms for peaceful space exploration.
• Debate over a new UN world map’s color schemes irked several nations, illustrating how cartography can ripple into diplomacy.
Why it matters: Competing power blocs, fragile waterways, and even symbolism on maps illustrate how norms and access—on Earth and in space—shape global influence.

Artificial Intelligence
• Anthropic reported thwarting attempts to misuse AI models for biological research and alleged systematic “distillation” efforts by China-based labs to improve rival systems.
• OpenAI paused new sign-ups for Pro amid surging demand for its Astra agent and is exploring whether coordinating an industry slowdown could be legal under antitrust rules.
• Meta’s Muse assistant rapidly climbed U.S. app charts, while Universal Music and ElevenLabs unveiled an AI music platform to enable licensed remixes and mashups.
• A potential data sale out of Spirit’s bankruptcy to Google triggered alarm over how AI firms source training data.
Why it matters: Rapid adoption, rising misuse risks, and unresolved data-rights questions are converging as AI moves deeper into core services and creative industries.

Entertainment
• TIFF opened with Siân Heder’s “Being Heumann,” a disability-rights drama that drew strong early notices and positioned Apple for awards buzz.
• Charli XCX announced a six-date 2027 U.K. and Europe arena run, while the VMAs unveiled nominations and named Nirvana as Video Vanguard honoree.
• Princess Diana’s “revenge dress” heads to auction at Sotheby’s with estimates up to $300,000; Snapchat launched “Plans” to turn group chats into in-app events.
Why it matters: Festivals, legacy icons, and platform features reflect how cultural narratives and audience engagement are evolving across film, music, and social apps.

Armed Conflict & Security
• Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis seized the Red Sea port of Mokha, tightening control over a key maritime route near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
• Philippine rescuers boarded a ferry more than 40 hours after a deadly blaze; dozens remain missing as hazardous conditions hamper efforts.
• Ukraine accused Russia of escalating strikes on civilian infrastructure, as Kremlin rhetoric raised nuclear threats toward NATO-member Lithuania.
• A report alleged Houthis attempted to use Anthropic’s AI to aid ballistic missile development, highlighting the limits of AI safeguards.
Why it matters: Control of strategic waterways, civilian targeting, and AI’s dual-use risks are reshaping security challenges from the Red Sea to Eastern Europe.

Economy & Markets
• U.S. diesel hit a record $6/gal amid Iran-related supply shocks, while the IEA warned the Hormuz closure could depress oil demand even as refined products surge in price.
• The UK economy unexpectedly grew 0.4% in July, with AI-driven services offsetting war-related headwinds.
• The U.S.–Canada trade war is snarling integrated auto-parts supply chains, amplifying cost and logistics risks.
• Bond markets steadied after a global sell-off, but investors warned U.S. Treasury operations haven’t cooled rising borrowing costs.
Why it matters: Energy price shocks, AI-linked productivity pockets, and fragile debt dynamics are shaping growth prospects and inflation risks across advanced economies.

Climate & Environment
• Hurricane Lowell battered Hawaii’s western islands with widespread outages and infrastructure damage, amid questions about rising storm exposure.
• A new roadmap proposes experiments and governance steps to inform decisions on solar geoengineering.
• Nearly half of migratory bird species are in decline, with one in nine threatened with extinction, per a global assessment.
• UK ministers are weighing higher water prices for industrial users to address shortages; chemical giants agreed to a $455m PFAS settlement in North Carolina.
Why it matters: Intensifying climate impacts, contested techno-fixes, biodiversity loss, and resource constraints are forcing faster policy choices and accountability.

Science & Technology
• The FAA-backed eVTOL pilot program begins Texas test flights for electric and autonomous air taxis ahead of finalized rules.
• Europe will press ahead with its Venus mission after the U.S. withdrew a key radar instrument, potentially shifting partnerships.
• NASA’s Chandra telescope spotted new faint X-ray objects bright in UV, offering clues to astrophysical mysteries; researchers also suggested dark energy may be evolving based on a 3,000-supernova catalog.
• NASA advanced its Space Academy initiative as Artemis II astronauts moved to “emeritus” status, signaling shifting human-spaceflight plans.
Why it matters: From next-gen aviation to deep-space science, shifting alliances and discoveries are redrawing the frontiers of transportation and cosmology.

Health & Pandemic
• Record UK heatwaves drove the NHS’s busiest summer on record and forced cancellation of more than 1,000 operations, highlighting climate’s strain on health systems.
• Research-backed microhabits—short, consistent mindfulness practices—can match longer sessions in boosting wellbeing.
• Doctors reported a “toasted skin” syndrome in a child from prolonged laptop heat exposure, a reminder of subtle tech-related health risks.
Why it matters: Climate stress, behavioral science, and everyday technology are intersecting in new ways to challenge and improve public health.

Art & Culture
• TikTok is reshaping English usage, with common verbs taking on new functions and meanings across social media.
• At Venice’s Final Cut, Congolese filmmaker Machérie Ekwa Bahango urged broader recognition of Congo’s stories and agency in global cinema.
• Bruce Springsteen defended his politically themed tour as a candid portrait of America, even at the cost of alienating some fans.
Why it matters: Platform-driven language shifts and artists foregrounding underrepresented narratives show culture’s power to redefine identity and discourse.

Longevity & Anti-Aging
• Researchers emphasize large person-to-person variance in aging trajectories—even with similar genetics and lifestyles—complicating universal treatment approaches.
• New work links calcium mishandling in muscle cells to age-related weakness, suggesting targets to slow sarcopenia.
• Madrid prepares to host a major longevity gathering aimed at translating scientific momentum into broader public health gains.
Why it matters: As the science matures, personalized strategies and mechanistic insights are key to extending healthy years—not just lifespan.

Entertainment.title: H//PE Princess Is Breaking the Rules of Girls-Group Music
Entertainment.text: When Mnet’s joint Korean-Japanese audition program Unpretty Rapstar: HIP POP Princess wrapped up, it birthed a seven-member global entity determined to break every convention in girls-group  music. Operating under the name H//PE Princess, COCO, YSY, YUJU, DOI, RINO, NIKO and SUJIN officially launched on May 27, 2026, with their debut mini-album 17.7 — a direct reference to the members’ average age when the group first assembled.The group's immediate impact was solidified through major breakout tracks -- their lead single "Stolen," produced by Dynamicduo's Gaeko, exploded past 1 million views within 24 hours of release, while "One day," written and produced by ONE OK ROCK frontman Taka, racked up millions of views within one week. Together with audition fan-favorites like "DAISY" and "gOOd!," these releases fueled a rapid ascent that carried H//PE Princess to major international stages like Rakuten GirlsAward and KCON.Fresh off their whirlwind promotions, we spoke with H//PE Princess to discuss life after their debut, the symbolic meaning behind their name, and how they plan to forge their own path in global music.It’s been about two months since H//PE Princess officially stepped into the spotlight. How has daily life changed for you all since debuting?NIKO: It’s been so exciting to connect with fans through social media and really let people get to know who we are. We’re also getting to perform on so many different stages - festivals, TV shows, university events - and every time we step out there, it finally hits me: “Wow, we’re really H//PE Princess now.” Experiencing that love and support firsthand in our new daily lives is something we’re deeply grateful for, and it makes every day so much fun.DOI: Life has been an absolute whirlwind. I’m constantly practicing, studying and pushing myself to grow every single day. If I had to pick the biggest shift since our debut, it’s definitely the fact that we’re continuously on stage now. Being able to show so many people who we are as artists is something I’m genuinely thankful for.Let's talk about your group name, H//PE Princess. What's the meaning behind the double slashes, and how does the name reflect your visual and musical identity?YUJU: The name represents our desire to fill the space between those double slashes with our own story. It’s about transcending boundaries - specifically between Korean and Japanese cultures, languages and ideas - and breaking through limits altogether. Both on and off stage, we’re working hard to refine our individual branding while carving out a crystal-clear identity as a team.RINO: To me, the space between the slashes is a canvas where we can freely expand our possibilities without being boxed in. Instead of confining ourselves to a single genre - whether that’s K-pop, J-pop, or hip-hop - we want to blend our individual backgrounds to create something that feels distinctly H//PE Princess. Beyond music genres and geographical borders, it’s about breaking away from predefined expectations of who we’re "supposed" to be and building our own authentic identity.The K-pop landscape moves at such a rapid pace. What do you feel is the core element that sets H//PE Princess’s sound and energy apart from other new groups?YSY: What sets H//PE Princess apart is that all seven of us have very distinct, vivid personalities — each member brings a completely different flavor to the group. We also place huge importance on raw energy and live performance skills. Whenever the setup allows, we always insist on using handheld mics because we’re that confident in our live vocals and stage presence. We have confidence in our live performance, and I think that energy is our biggest charm.COCO: Performing with handheld mics allows each member’s voice, expression and raw emotion to reach the audience directly. Instead of squeezing seven people into a rigid mold, we bring seven completely different colors together to build a sound from scratch. That chemistry - the explosive energy when our individual styles mesh on stage - is something only H//PE Princess can deliver.If you had to describe the overall vibe and ethos of H//PE Princess in just three words, what would they be?SUJIN: Composure, Confidence, and Duality.YUJU:  Unbound, Diverse, and One-of-a-kind.Each of you brought a different background and musical taste into the trainee room. How did those individual styles blend when shaping the group’s collective identity?COCO: Rather than trying to erase our differences or force ourselves into a uniform mold, we created our music while embracing everyone’s individual style. We all have different musical tastes and ways of expressing ourselves, so brainstorming during practice naturally sparked fresh ideas. Our identity isn’t defined by a single person’s aesthetic — it’s the harmony of seven distinct colors blending together.YUJU: At first, because everyone’s personality is so distinct, I thought finding a cohesive direction might be tough. But I quickly realized that when we lean into our individual strengths and harmonize, we become an even more unique and unrivaled group. By respecting and building off one another’s styles, we’re creating a fresh aesthetic that belongs exclusively to H//PE Princess.Now that you’ve checked off your official debut, what’s the next major goal on H//PE Princess’s bucket list for your first year?SUJIN: Debuting officially is really just the beginning of a whole new challenge. Our biggest goal for this first year is to grind, practice relentlessly and carve out a signature sound so the public clearly recognizes what H//PE Princess brings to the table.YSY: The seven of us achieved our dream of debuting, but now we’re standing at the starting line of an even bigger journey. Since H//PE Princess was formed through an audition show, it’s up to us to go out there and prove what kind of artists we really are. Through every stage and performance, we want to show our potential, grow step by step, and pave a lane that’s entirely our own.Looking ahead to future releases, are there any specific genres, visual concepts, or sonic styles you’re itching to experiment with next?NIKO: While we want to explore diverse genres, we’re focused on solidifying our identity as a hip-hop group even further. Beyond the music, we want to take ownership of our styling, visuals, and performances to build a self-produced aesthetic that only H//PE Princess can execute. Moving forward, we want to push the envelope with bolder, higher-impact concepts and bring our vision into sharper focus.DOI: Hip-hop is our root, but we’re eager to branch out into electronic music and R&B. We love old-school hip-hop, but we never want to be boxed into just one sound. We want to keep experimenting across different genres to show all the different dimensions of H//PE Princess.Image source (C) CJ ENM ﻿Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Entertainment.title: Josh Hartnett Battles a Terrifying Sea Creature in Upcoming Netflix Series 'Below'
Entertainment.text: SummaryNetflix has released the official trailer for its upcoming limited drama series 'Below'Josh Hartnett stars as a Newfoundland fisherman confronting a deadly sea creature lurking off the coastCreated by Jesse McKeown the six-part thriller debuts October 8 following its TIFF premiereNetflix has officially unveiled the trailer for its upcoming drama series, Below. The six-part limited series stars Josh Hartnett and is set to make its world premiere at the Toronto International Film Festival before launching on the streaming platform.Set off the coast of Newfoundland, the story follows Calvin Penney (Hartnett), a stubborn small-town fisherman haunted by the mysterious death of his father decades prior. When a terrifying, unidentified sea creature begins terrorizing the local waters, Calvin is forced into action. He teams up with a visiting marine researcher (Mackenzie Davis) to protect his son Wade (Charlie Heaton) and his community, racing to uncover the island's buried secrets before it's too late.Created by Jesse McKeown, the project blends local mythology, suspense, and humor to explore deeper themes of family, community, and change. The ensemble cast features Ruby Stokes, Kaleb Horn, Rohan Campbell, and Willow Kean. Executive production is handled by Jessica Rhoades, Chris Hatcher, Jamie Childs, Louise Sutton, Sharon Hall, and Hartnett.Below will officially launch globally on Netflix on October 8, 2026.Read more at Hypebeast

Economy & Markets.title: McLaren Reveals Plans for an 810 HP Hybrid P34 Supercar, an SUV, and a Luxury Brand Overhaul
Economy & Markets.text: SummaryMcLaren briefed retailers on a future product roadmap highlighted by a new 810-horsepower hybrid V-6 supercarThe automaker plans to ditch its clinical dealership aesthetic to mimic luxury fashion boutiques like Gucci and Louis VuittonA long-rumored SUV and a front-engined grand tourer are slated for release further down the production timelineMcLaren is officially drawing up the blueprint for its next era, pivoting its identity from a performance manufacturer to a lifestyle powerhouse. During a recent confidential briefing with its retail network, the British automaker outlined a future product roadmap alongside sweeping changes to its brand aesthetic. Showroom floor transformations represent the most immediate cultural shift. Dealerships are slated for a massive redesign, ditching their current Apple-store-like aesthetic in favor of the opulent ambiance found in luxury fashion stores like Gucci, Louis Vuitton or Burberry. This transformation of retail spaces represents a deliberate strategic pivot to reposition McLaren against high-end lifestyle brands by relying on elite luxury aesthetics rather than just track-day supremacy.The tip of the spear for this incoming product wave is a highly anticipated mid-engined supercar currently operating under the code-named P34. Expected to arrive next summer, the vehicle will be propelled by a hybridized twin-turbo V-6 powertrain. This setup is similar to the system found in the Artura, effectively moving the brand away from its long-lived V-8 engine. Despite the shift in configuration, the output remains entirely uncompromising. The upcoming P34 will reportedly push out approximately 810 horsepower and 800 pound-feet of torque. Slated to slot cleanly between the Artura and the 750S in the McLaren vehicle lineup, the hybrid supercar is expected to carry a starting price of around $310,000, deliberately undercutting the MSRP of the 750S.To match the company's new lifestyle directive, the P34 aims to deliver serious physical and technological upgrades. The exterior shape of the new supercar will reportedly be longer and more dramatic than the current Artura profile. Inside the cabin, the automaker is leaning heavily into its luxury-focused identity. New leather seats and an array of updated LED screens will outfit the interior of the P34, a direct maneuver to better compete with rival high-end luxury brands. Anticipating strong demand for this modernized package, McLaren reportedly plans to build about 1,000 copies of the supercar during its first year of production alone.While the P34 represents the immediate future, the automaker's long-term plans include even more disruptive additions to its catalog. The brand's pipeline also calls for a "sedan-like" front-engined grand tourer as well as a long-rumored SUV. Redesigning dealerships, the SUV and the grand tourer are all slated to arrive further out in the timeline than the P34. Venturing into these broader, passenger-friendly vehicle segments is a critical move for the brand's financial longevity. Michael Leiters, a former executive at the company, stated in 2024 that an SUV or a grand tourer would be major keys to future profitability. Naturally, the automaker is keeping its official cards close to the chest. A McLaren spokesperson declined to comment to Road & Track regarding the report, simply stating the brand does not comment on speculation.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Science & Technology.title: Codeveloper of Ethernet Predecessor Dies at 91
Science & Technology.text: Franklin “Frank” KuoCodeveloper of ALOHAnetFellow, 91; died 14 AprilKuo helped develop ALOHAnet, a pioneering computer system at the University of Hawaii at Mānoa, in Honolulu. The system went online in 1971 and represented the first public demonstration of a wireless packet data network. It was an inspiration for Robert Metcalfe’s development of Ethernet a couple of years later. In 2020 ALOHAnet was designated as an IEEE Milestone.Kuo earned bachelor’s, master’s, and doctoral degrees in electrical engineering from the University of Illinois, Urbana-Champaign. After earning his Ph.D. in 1960, he joined Bell Labs in Murray Hill, N.J., where he conducted research in computer communications.After six years at the company, Kuo left to become a professor of electrical engineering at the University of Hawaii. From 1968 to 1971 he and one of his colleagues, IEEE Life Fellow Norman Abramson, developed ALOHAnet. The network connected computers on Hawaiian islands using ultrahigh-frequency radio, transmitting information over radio waves instead of cables.ALOHAnet became the foundation for modern networks. Kuo pioneered the concept of a random-access protocol, or sharing a single channel without central coordination—which led to the packet-switching principles that underpin modern Wi-Fi and mobile networks.Kuo authored or coauthored several books including Computer Communication Networks. Published in 1972, it was one of the earliest textbooks on the subject.He served as director of the university’s Cosine committee, a project funded by the U.S. National Science Foundation to develop computer engineering courses.He took a sabbatical from 1975 to 1977 to work at the U.S. Pentagon as director of information systems in the defense secretary’s office. He oversaw computer communications applications used in command, control, and intelligence programs.During the 1980s and ’90s, he helped develop China’s Internet. In 1982 he joined SRI International (formerly the Stanford Research Institute), in Menlo Park, Calif., as a researcher. He also was a consulting professor in Stanford’s electrical engineering department and taught computer networking at Shanghai Jiao Tong University.As a UNESCO lecturer in Beijing in 1994, he helped Peking University, Tsinghua University, and the Chinese Academy of Sciences connect to the Internet. He also worked with Tsinghua University to develop CERNET, the country’s first nationwide education and research computer network, which was managed by the Chinese Ministry of Education. For his work, he received an honorary degree from Shanghai Jiao Tong University.In the mid-1990s, Kuo helped found General Wireless Communications, a developer of mobile phone messaging services and games that was renamed Mtone Wireless.Muhammad Rezaul KarimBell Labs researcherLife senior member, 86; died 18 MayKarim was a distinguished member of the technical staff at Bell Labs in Murray Hill, N.J. His work was instrumental in the development of modern cellular communications technology.He joined Bell Labs in 1972 and worked in its mobile telecommunications laboratory as part of the team tasked with creating one of the earliest cellular networks.In 1975 Illinois Bell Telephone petitioned the U.S. Federal Communications Commission to develop and test a cellular system. The FCC, which now regulates radio, TV, telephone, Internet, satellite, and wireless services, authorized the project in March 1977. Karim and his team helped develop key elements of the technology, including the Bell Labs logic that controlled the cellular system, turning the concept into a working one. They also built radio receivers, transmitters, control systems, and cell-site equipment used in the first trial of the cellular system.The following year, Bell Labs and Illinois Bell deployed the Advanced Mobile Phone Service system across Chicago, with its switching office located in Oak Park, Ill. The initial test used approximately 100 mobile phones to work through hardware, software, and system-design problems.A subsequent test in 1979 involved 2,500 mobile users, providing a demonstration of the cellular technology in practice.The trials in Illinois helped establish the technical foundation for the commercial cellular networks that followed.Later in his career, Karim worked on the asynchronous transfer mode (ATM) technique, a high-speed networking technology crucial to the transition from traditional telephone networks to broadband and digital ones.In 2000 he published ATM Networks: Application, Systems, and Design, a textbook that served as a guide for designing and implementing ATM-based services.Karim received a bachelor’s degree in electrical engineering from the Bangladesh University of Engineering and Technology, in Dhaka. He then earned a master’s degree in EE from the University of Manchester, England, and a Ph.D. in EE from Stevens Institute of Technology, in Hoboken, N.J.Harry BosticFormer IEEE Region 4 directorLife senior member, 86; died 18 MarchBostic was an active IEEE volunteer who served as the 1998–1999 director of IEEE Region 4. In 2007 he received a lifetime achievement award from the IEEE Central Indiana Section for “outstanding commitment and dedicated service as regional advisor to the volunteers and members of Region 4 and the Institute.”He was an engineer for 30 years at U.S. Navy’s avionics facility, a research, development, and manufacturing concern in Indianapolis. He worked on flight control, navigation, and weapons systems there. (The facility closed in 1996.)Edwin C. Jones Jr.ProfessorLife Fellow, 91; died 10 MarchJones was widely recognized for his contributions to engineering education, curriculum development, and accreditation through decades of service to IEEE, ABET, and the American Society for Engineering Education.He earned a bachelor’s degree in electrical engineering in 1955 from West Virginia University in Morgantown. The following year he earned a diploma of membership (equivalent to a master’s degree) from Imperial College, London. He went on to serve in the U.S. Army Signal Corps for two years. After his service ended, he studied engineering education at the University of Illinois, Urbana-Champaign, earning a Ph.D. in 1961. Jones then joined the university’s faculty.The following year, he left Illinois to join Iowa State University, in Ames, as an assistant professor. He was promoted to professor in 1995. Two years later he became associate chair of the electrical and computer engineering department and served in that position until 2001, when he retired and was named professor emeritus. In recognition of his commitment to students, Iowa State established a scholarship in his honor.In 2006 he accepted a part-time position as an adjunct professor in Minnesota at the University of St. Thomas, in St. Paul. He advised graduate students and helped develop the university’s systems engineering program.An active IEEE volunteer, he served as 1975–1976 president of the IEEE Education Society. He was a member of the IEEE Educational Activities Board, helping strengthen the relationship among engineering education, professional practice, and accreditation organizations. He received an IEEE Centennial Medal in 1984 and the EAB Meritorious Achievement Award in Accreditation Activities in 1986. The IEEE Education Society later named its Meritorious Service Award in his honor.Jones was elected a Fellow of ABET in 1986. During his years of service as a program evaluator and leader, he helped advance the quality of engineering education and accreditation programs. ABET recognized him with its Grinter Distinguished Service Award, its highest honor.Alexander Robert SpitzerClinical neurology researcherLife senior member, 70; died 27 FebruarySpitzer was a neurologist for 40 years at the Wayne State University School of Medicine, in Detroit, where he also was a director of the electromyography laboratory at Harper University Hospital. The lab studied patients’ brain and spinal cord activity in response to sensory stimuli. The evaluations assessed nerve pathway integrity to help diagnose multiple sclerosis, spinal cord injuries, and other conditions.After earning his medical degree from the Einstein College of Medicine, in New York City, Spitzer completed a fellowship at the U.S. National Institutes of Health, in Bethesda, Md. He then joined Wayne State as a clinical neurology researcher. His pioneering research in applying neural network analysis to electromyography and clinical neurophysiology resulted in peer-reviewed publications, grants, and several U.S. patents.He mentored generations of neurologists in electrodiagnostic medicine, a medical specialty that uses nerve-conduction and electromyography tests to evaluate and diagnose muscle and nerve disorders.In 2020 he founded Mackinac Neurology, a telemedicine-based practice that treated pa­tients virtually during the COVID-19 pandemic.A longtime IEEE volunteer, he held numerous roles on the IEEE Regional Activities Board, now known as the Member and Geographic Activities Board. He was a member of the IEEE Ethics and Member Conduct and Nominations and Appointments committees, as well as the IEEE Educational Activities and IEEE-USA boards. He served as 1977–1979 director of the IEEE Central Indiana Section.Donald Leo DietmeyerProfessorLife Fellow, 93; died 13 FebruaryDietmeyer was a professor of electrical and computer engineering for 40 years at the University of Wisconsin-Madison.He developed a lifelong interest in radio and electronics at high school in Wausau, Wisc., and earned a Ph.D. in electrical engineering in 1959 from the University of Wisconsin. He’d joined the university’s electrical engineering faculty as a professor in 1958 while pursuing his doctorate.Dietmeyer’s research focused on computer-aided design in the areas of switching theory, hardware description languages, and the decomposition of Boolean functions. His research contributed to the development of automation tools for integrated circuit design.He worked with Jim Duley, a former student, to pioneer the use of the digital system design language. He wrote the textbook Logic Design of Digital Systems, published in 1978.In the early 1980s, Dietmeyer worked with researchers to develop ConLan, a language-construction method that combined hardware description languages in one underlying framework.He served as associate dean of the University of Wisconsin’s electrical and computer engineering department from 1983 to 1995. In 1998 he retired and was named professor emeritus.

Art & Culture.title: Uchronia Brings Fluid Curves and Glitter Finishes to Tiptoe’s Signature Furniture
Art & Culture.text: SummaryTiptoe x Uchronia unveil their "DAYDREAM" collection at Paris Design Week 2026, reworking Tiptoe’s iconic furniture.The collection features wave‑like contours and four exclusive colors blending art and function.Launch at Grand Palais, highlighting sustainability and emotional design innovation.French furniture brand Tiptoe and Parisian multidisciplinary collective Uchronia have joined forces to unveil "DAYDREAM," a vibrant collaborative collection debuting at the Grand Palais during Paris Design Week. Showcased within Uchronia's monumental "Le Grand Bouquet" installation, the capsule blends two distinct design philosophies: Tiptoe’s renowned industrial utility and Uchronia’s deeply poetic, sensory-driven universe.Described by Uchronia founder Julien Sebban as a "sensory, colour-driven journey," the "DAYDREAM" concept envisions a suspended dream state where everyday objects break free from their rigid forms, allowing contours to soften and colors to become a highly expressive, emotional language.Aesthetically, the collection transforms Tiptoe's signature steel hardware through a profound exploration of organic volume and vivid pigmentation. In stark contrast to the strictly geometric, minimalist lines that have defined Tiptoe's previous industrial iterations, this new capsule introduces fluid, wave-like curves inspired by the movement of water. This undulating motif softens the brand's historically rigid silhouettes, elevating functional homeware into sensory art objects. The visual language is further anchored by a bespoke palette of four exclusive, mood-inspired shades: a vibrant Magma Orange, a soft Ice Cream Beige, a nostalgic Chocolate Brown, and an Astral Purple that is uniquely flecked with fine stardust-like glitter to invite contemplation.Color plays a defining role in the collaboration, with Uchronia developing a palette of four exclusive shades: Magma Orange, a vibrant signature hue; Ice Cream Beige, soft and luminous; Astral Violet, deep with pearlescent highlights; and Chocolate Brown, nostalgic and comforting. These tones are applied across reworked surfaces and sculpted wood tabletops, each ripple carefully cut to respect the grain and natural nobility of the material. The result is a collection that feels both playful and contemplative, inviting users to experience furniture as part of an inner landscape.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Longevity & Anti-Aging.title: Aging is Complex, So Expect High Variance in the Details Between Individuals
Longevity & Anti-Aging.text: Aging is a complex stochastic process of damage accumulation, shaped at the detail level by choices made, environments encountered, and the responses and interactions of countless cells. As the paper here notes, this gives rise to a sizable variance between individuals, even those with the same genetics or similar lifestyles. The research and medical community largely react to this variance with a drive towards developing personalized medicine, but the underlying mechanisms of aging are the same from individual to individual, even if outcomes vary. A therapy that addresses one underlying mechanism in one tissue will tend to produce differing levels of benefit from person to person, but in principle it should always produce benefit.
